Section agreed to on division.
On section 5-Salaries to be paid from first appointment:

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext:
I think, from the disclosure made by the parliamentary undersecretary of state for External Affairs (Mr. Hugh Clark) this afternoon, this section should not be allowed to pass without protest. It is a most extraordinary thing that a minister of the Crown, as he is now by this retroactive legislation, should be obliged to admit here that instead of attending to the affairs of the country for which he is paid a fairly high salary of $5,000 a year, together with his indemnity, he is devoting his time to preparing literature in the interest of the Conservative party and of the Government. It is not a fair, square deal that, while I myself and other hon members on this side of the House have to do our own work in election matters or otherwise and sustain our cause the best way we can, with our own efforts and our
4m

own little money, we should be -called upon to pay the salary of a man on the other side of the House who is doing the Tory work. A couple of years ago I was in the county of Victoria helping to conduct a local election. I found in that county-and the fact has never been denied by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) or any other .minister who had to do with the matter-that the whole system of telegraph lines with all its official staff was turned into a huge machinery for the conducting of the election on behalf of the Tory candidate. The matter was brought to the notice of the minister; it was admitted it was bad, but he never called upon the man in charge of the system to return the .moneys that had been collected. That is a case exactly similar to this, .where the money of the country, money that every one, Grit and Tory alike, contribute IS being used for election purposes. That is not fair. They had in that election a steamer, not only subsidized, but hired by the Government. The full cost of hiring the steamer and the full salaries of every officer aboard were paid by the Government of my right hon. friend. The steamboat, the officers and the whole outfit were used for at least a month, for the purpose of this election. I brought the matter to the notice of the Government and they said they were going to do something about it, but they never did anything. The officials received their pay; there was not even a reprimand given; it was regarded as just the proper thing to do. We are now going a step further. We are giving the dignity of the position of a minister of the Crown to a member of this House, and he has to acknowledge that, instead of doing anything that would be commensurate with the dignity of a minister of the Crown, he is grovelling down and muckraking for the purpose of slandering the Liberal party. That is the position for which we are voting him money. This purchasing of assistance of the press and otherwise with the public money is but a system and a policy adopted by this Government. The Government have bought the Halifax Herald. Hoes any one for a moment think that the gentleman who owned the Halifax Herald would have been made a senator and his paper bought were it not for the fact that he owned that paper? Nobody in the world would ever think so, or would accuse the Prime Minister of making such an appointment, were it not for the fact that, by buying the Herald, he had to take this appendage with it. The same thing happened in the county of Cape 
breton, a part of which I represent. In the city of Sydney we have the Post, a good Tory paper. It had to be bought.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: There are some good Tory papers?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Good of their kind. It had to be brought into line. It was deeply in debt. It was stated on the authority of the gentleman who was bought with it that it was $95,000 behind in working up the interest of the Tory party. The paper, however, was bought and with it the same sort of appendage a3 in the case of the Halifax Herald. Eight in line comes the Bill that is before us to-night. It is said that the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) wanted to be Speaker. Two men could not be Speaker ait the same time, and when the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) was made Speaker, of course something had to be done for the hon. member (Mr. McCurdy), and so lie was appointed Parliamentary Secretary to the Department of Militia and Defence with a salary of $5,000. It is a well known fact that the hon. member for North Bruce [Mr. Hugh Clark) was going around bis countysaying that he had the promise of the Pi line Minister that he would be appointed Minister of Militia. He was nor appointed Minister of Militia, hut over his bead, when the lime came and the ex-Min:?te.r of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) went out, the hon. member for East Toronto (Sir Edward Kemp), the present holder, was appointed. The hon. member for North Bruce, of course, to whom this offer, according to himself, was promised, was very much disgruntled and disappointed, and something had to be done for him, and iso he was. appointed Parliamentary Under-Secretary of Stat-e for External Affairs. The country has to stand the brunt and pay the money.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: He voted for himself.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext:
Charity begins at
home, and for that reason I do not want to blame him very much for voting for himself. He is the only real democrat in the crowd, and I sympathize with him. He is willing to take the money openly and above board, the others want to get it by some circuitous route, but they will get it all the same.
Mr. MeCURDY: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to apply that remark to me? Does he say the other parliamentary secretaries want to take the money by some circuitous route?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: A guilty conscience needs no accuser.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I rise to a point of order, and I ask that the insinuation be withdrawn. I have no intention of taking remuneration for this office in any shape or form, and I think the hon. gentleman should withdraw.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I said nothing to withdraw.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Why did my hon. friend vote for it?

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Did my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) vote for an increase in the parliamentary indemnity? it is the same thing.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: The hon. member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) is an old parliamentarian, and should take the word of the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne-

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I did not say a word to him, not a word. There is an old story about a man who was in a court house-

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Withdraw.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I see that Rome is saved once more by cackle of the same old class.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Withdraw.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Withdraw what? I was simply going to refer to a gentleman who was pointed out as a man with a fly on his nose. Of course, there was no fly on his nose, but he thought there was. If the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) is the man with the fly on his nose-I cannot help it.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. If I understood the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) aright, he insinuated that I wished to take this money by a circuitous route. I regard these words as entirely objectionable, and I would ask that they be withdrawn.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I did not say at all that the hon. member was taking the money. There are thousands of such cases in Canada, and I say others take it by a circuitous route, as well as the hon. member. .

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Question.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Withdraw.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: What am I going to withdraw? I stand by the point that when people get money in an indirect way, it would be very much more honest and becoming for them to take it straight as it is voted for them. I have seen hundreds of them saying they were doing work for nothing, and when the accounts came in afterwards they amounted to ten times more than they would have if they were taking the money straight. If people are so very sensitive, it would be better for them not to be voting money to themselves, which they are not going to take. That is the question before the committee.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: Withdraw.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I will not withdraw anything. I have nothing to withdraw.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext:
The hon. member
should, I think, withdraw the insinuation that the hon. member fctr Queens and Shelburne would draw his money in an indirect way. The hon. member (Mr. McCurdy) has denied it.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I was speaking of the principle.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) intended to convey, but he certainly did convey to the members of the committee the direct insinuation that the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy), while pretending he would not accept this money, intended to get it by some indirect way. He either meant that or he meant nothing, and I believe the hon. gentleman cannot get out of it. I think he knows perfectly well he did mean that. It seems co me a very unworthy thing for the hon. gentleman to state. He has either said too much or too little. If he has anything upon which he can found an insinuation of that kind he should state it, if he has' nothing upon which to found it then he should withdraw.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I did not mean that the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne would get the money in any dishonest way, but it is my belief, whether it is proper or not, that he is not going to serve the country for nothing, and that directly or indirectly he will be paid for any services he gives the country. If there is anything unparliamentary in what I said before, I regret it and I take it back, but I believe we are not getting any services from anybody for nothing

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I do not think the committee is very much edified by the observations my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) hag seen fit to make. He has charged the Parliamentary Secretary for External Affairs with devoting his time altogether to preparing campaign literature, and has distorted what was said this afternoon into a supposed admission of that. It would be just as fair for me to distort what the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) said this afternoon into a supposed admission that when he was Minister of Railways and Canals he spent the whole of his time in writing editorials for Liberal newspapers. I would not for a momem suggest anything of that kind, and no hon. member would suggest anything of the kind, yet it would be absolutely on a par with what my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has suggested with regard to the Parliamentary Under-Secretary for External Affairs. Where does my hon. friend draw the line? Does he censure the hon. member for South Renfrew for writing editorials for his newspaper when he was Minister of Railways and Canals? Would he censure the hon. gentleman for writing a letter to a newspaper upon a political question? Would he censure him for making a speech-

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: If the Prime Minister expects me to give him any answer, I would say I certainly would not find fault with any one who runs a newspaper writing articles for his paper, but I would find fault if he was receiving a salary from the country and doing other work than that for which he was paid by the Crown.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext:
It strikes me my hon. friend is drawing an exceedingly fine distinction when he says that a gentleman can occupy a position in the public service as Minister of Railways and Canals, and can without censure or criticism devote his time to writing partisan editorials, but that the Parliamentary Under-Secretary for External Affairs is to be condemned because he writes letters either for his own newspaper or to some other newspaper defending the Administration and perhaps having a partisan tinge. I must confess I do not understand the distinction my hon. friend is making, and I do not think he has edified the committee very much by the observations with which he has favoured it. This is simply a clause which provides that those gentlemen shall be entitled to a certain salary for the period during which they have held certain offices and discharged certain duties. It places the moneys at their disposal. If they decline to accept,

it is their own affair. If they accept the salary and devote it to some public or patriotic purpose, that is a matter for their own judgment. If they accept and devote it to their own personal purposes, it is their right under the legislation. That Jso is a matter for themselves. This is all the section means.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: How long will they have to accept? Will they he governed by the Statute of Limitations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext: I do not think that that is of very much interest.

maintopic: MINISTER OF OVERSEAS MILITARY FORCES AND PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES.
speechtext:
My right hon. friend is rather to bepitied than otherwise, if he is unable, to draw a distinction between a gentleman who is now being appointed to an office at a salary of $5,000 a year, and for whom the office is being created, who is devoting his time to the preparation of campaign literature in the interests of his political party, and the case of a man who, being a minister simply writes editorials for a newspaper which happens to be his own private property.
I am very sorry to hear it practically admitted by the Prime Minister that the gentleman who has been appointed Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs is really engaged in preparing campaign literature in order to promote the interests Of the Government and the Conservative party in the coming election. I have noticed that during the election that the hon. gentleman has never apparently given any evidence that he is doing any work in connection with his department. speakerposition: topic
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Mr. Rogers, the House went into committee on the following proposed resolutions; Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Dry Docks Subsidies Act, 1910, be amended by increasing the subsidy on first-class dry docks to four and one-half per cent of the cost of the work, payable half-yearly during a period not exceeding thirty-five years after the work has been completed, but half-yearly payments on account of the subsidy at the rate of four and one-half per cent on seventy-five per cent of the cost of the work done and materials provided at the time of such payment may be made during the construction of the dock, no such payment to be made until the work done and materials provided shall have cost the sum of five hundred thousand dollars, and no such payments on account to be made unless the chief engineer reports that the work is being proceeded with to his satisfaction.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
There is one provision
in the resolution which I am very glad the hon. minister is asking the House to agree to; that is increasing the rate of interest from four to four and a half per cent.	As a	reason for	this, it
might perhaps be desirable to refer for a few minutes to the history of the. aid to dry docks. My first knowledge of the matter was in 1882, when the Government asked Parliament to grant aid, somewhat along these lines, not in the way of an Act to provide for a subsidy to he paid in cash, like the subsidies to railways, but in the nature of a subsidy extending over a period of years. From that time to the present very little of an effective character, so far as Telates to the country at large, has been accomplished by the legislation. My experience has rather been that all the . Governments from that time down to the present-and I am disposed to include the Government of which I was a member- while improving a little upon the previous legislation, were just a little behind the requirements of the investor, to enable anything practicable to result from the resolution. First, the rate of interest was three per cent, then three and a half, and then four, and now it is proposed to make it four and a half, but to-day four and a half per cent is not very much better than three and a half per cent was some few years ago, *because the interest rate is higher. We know that even the Government cannot borrow to-day at less than six per cent, and many exceedingly good municipal securities are being sold on the market at six per cent. This class of aid is not very attractive security for the investor, because there is no security for the principal. It
merely secures the interest at what, to-day, is a low rate, four and a half per cent for .thirty-five years, but the investor has no guarantee that his principal will ever be paid. I suppose that is why the investor has not taken very kindly to the securities of drydocks companies. However, the increasing of the rate to four and a half may lead to something practical. I think, in regard to the aid which may be given in respect of the work while construction is going on, that the payment should be limited to an expenditure of, at least, a million dollars. I suggest that we should make it a million dollars, instead of $500,000, and make the half-yearly payments on seventy-five per cent of that amount. I think that, if that is provided for, and the Engineering Department is satisfied, whatever subsidy is given upon the expenditure should continue for the thirty-five years. Of course, it might be said, in answer to that, that possibly the drydock might be started, and might not be completed, and the Government would have the work on its hands. That is true, but that applies also to railways. We know that Parliament for many years has been granting aid during construction, I think after ten miles have been constructed, or after forty per cent of the work has been completed, the department will take progress estimates, and make payments on account. I do not see why the same provision should not be made applicable to drydocks, provided they are, as this resolution stipulates, of the first class, and if they are in parts of the country where a drydock of the first class is needed in the public interest. I think the building of drydocks, and the construction of ships in connection with them, which can be very greatly encouraged by reason of the plant for repair work that is necessary in connection with docks, is of enormous importance. There never was a time, and perhaps there never will be, in the history of the country, when it is more desirable, in the public interest, to secure the early establishment of shipyards in Canada. My hon. friend will agree with me when I say the war may last for some years yet, and the question of shipbuilding appeals to every man in the country as being of very vital importance. I suggest to the hon. minister that after the word " may," in the seventh line of the resolution, we insert the words " in respect to work done." I also suggest that we fix the amount at $1,000,000, so that the money invested will be so large as to be a pretty
445u

good assurance that the whole of the work will be completed, and if, for any reason, there were any stoppage, the Government would have a margin of $250,000. I would provide in the Bill that, in case of any default, the Government take charge and become the owner of any work done. I suggest, for the minister's favourable consideration, that we should strike out of the resolution the following words:
And no such payments on account to be made unless the chief engineer reports that the work Is being proceeded with to his satisfaction.
iln connection with securing money for a dry dock costing $4,000,000 or $5,000,000, and for the necessary repair plant and shipbuilding plant-I should like to see the latter established in connection with every dry dock that is constructed-in these days when the rate of interest is high and many favoured investments are offering, a banker would not look with very much favour upon bonds issued during construction unless in respect to those bonds the subsidy was to run for the period specified in the Bill. There is no use in passing legislation that is not going to procure results. As I say, I speak from having been interested in St. John in securing the building of a dry dock; that interest began thirty-five years ago, and there is no dry dock yet. Parliament always did pretty nearly what the investor wanted-but not quite. There is no use in putting legislation on the statute book unless it is of such a character as reasonably to encourage investors. I would suggest that the lowest amount upon which subsidy shall be paid during construction be made $1,000,000. With the margin of 25 per cent, that would be $250,000 in respect to each payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend as to the importance of such legislation as will ensure the construction of dry docks wherever they are necessary and wherever their construction is feasible. It is true that at present there is greater need for dry docks than there has been hitherto, and it is true that the Dry Docks Subsidies Act, which has been on our statute books for some years, has not accomplished the purposes for which it was intended. That is due largely to the fact that the subsidies offered have not been sufficiently attractive. In bringing this resolution before Parliament, I thought that I was going a long way to remedy that condition. First of all,
I propose to increase the interest rate to
fMr. Pugsley.]
four and a half per cent. I propose also to remedy the complaint that has been made	whenever the
matter of the construction of dry docks was discussed in my department: that in connection with what are called progress Estimates. Under the old Dry Docks Subsidies Act, no estimate was given until the the dock was completed. I propose under this Bill to remedy that condition and to provide that we shall pay the subsidy on 75 per cent of the money spent. In .other words, when $500,000 is spent, we shall provide a subsidy half-yearly on $375,000 of the $500,000; and so on until the dock is completed. In this respect the Bill is a great improvement upon the previous legislation. Such an undertaking as the construction of a large dry dock of the first class is not usually promoted by contractors who are interested simply in the operation of a dry dock. I do not think the Act is workable except in cases where a corporation have in mind the establishing of a shipbuilding plant in connection with the dry dock; otherwise, I doubt whether the proposal, even under this legislation, would be sufficiently attractive to encourage the investment of so large XI p.m. an amount of money. But this legislation is certainly a great encouragement to any firm or company whigh has in mind the 'building of a shipbuilding plant and the carrying on of work of this kind. In St. John there is pressing necessity for the construction of a dry dock, especially at this time, when so many ships are coming into that port. The same applies to Halifax. While there is at Halifax a dock that has done splendid service, having regard to its capacity, yet in my judgment the accommodation is insufficient to meet the requirements of the trade. In the near future it will be necessary, under any legislation that we may enact, or in some other way, to provide a dry dock at that port. This is necessary not only because of the present requirements, but because of urgent requests made by the Admiralty and those interested in the shipping trade of our country. I do not know that I have great objection to the suggestion made by the member for St. John, because in introducing this resolution I had in view the one purpose of trying to present a measure that would he sufficiently attractive to produce some results under our Dry Docks Subsidy legislation. My hon. friend has suggested that the amount upon which subsidy should be paid should be made $1,000,000 instead of $500,000. I think

my hon. friend is in error in what he says with regard to railway subsidies. As I understand it, when a railway subsidy is granted and approved by Parliament it is understood that a certain number of miles of railway have to be constructed and that if that work is not carried out, the full subsidy is not paid.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
But they get paid
through the progress estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: We are proposing to pay them on progress estimate.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: Only the interest.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: How much does the minister estimate a complete first-class dry dock will cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
A first-class dry dock would probably cost something like $3,-
500,000	or perhaps $4,000,000. The Subsidy Act provides that we can grant a subsidy on a dry dock costing $5,000,000 a subsidy of $500,000, but that includes a subsidy on a shipbuilding plant connected with the dry dock. In respect to the change of the form of the subsidies to be granted, it has also been suggested that the subsidy should terminate at any time, so far as the contractors are concerned, should they fail to carry out their contract; but the suggestion is made that our Act should provide that supposing $1,000,000 has been expended on the construction of a dock, and the contractor fails after he has spent that amount and after we have paid him under the proposed arrangements, say, $750,000, all that should be exacted from him would be the loss of that $250,000 together with his deposit of $250,000 together as a guarantee of good faith that he would carry out the contract, and that we should' continue to pay the subsidy of 41 per cent upon the amount of money so put into the dock by the contractor.
Mr. A. K. MA'CLEAN: I suppose that is if the dock is completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: No, it is suggested that we should pay the subsidy provided the dock has not been completed. Even if the contractor had gone on to the extent of spending $1,000,000, if he failed to carry the work on to completion, we would be able to exact from him the $250,000 of the hold-back and the $250,000 of the deposit which he had put up as a guarantee of good faith that he would carry the work to completion.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: Do I understand that the Government will pay the interest on that amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: Not on that amount. We would pay the interest on the $750,000, because the contractor would in all probability borrow from some innocent investor the money to carry on the work up to this point. I am pointing out to the committee only what has been suggested.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: Does the minister say that we would continue to pay the interest on $750,000 for 35 years in the case of a dock that was not completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: No, but supposing a contractor had taken a contract and had borrowed $1,000,000, and under our Act we were obliged to pay a subsidy of $750,000 all told, and we had in addition his deposit of $250,000, and he fell down on his work, the suggestion is that we should pay the subsidy of the $750,000, and we should retain the other $500,000 and see that the contract is carried out by some other person and that the dock is completed and put into shape for the purpose for which it is intended. Although I am not clear as to the desirability of going as far as that, the suggestion deserves some consideration. In view of this, and in view of the fact that we are to have amendments to the resolution before the committee, it will be necessary for me to withdraw the resolution and bring in another one in keeping with the views of the committee. I would like, therefore, to get the judgment of members of the committee in order that I may know exactly their views on the subject. I am not wedded to any particular form or arrangement, but I am anxious that under this resolution we shall be able to get results and accomplish some good, because there is undoubtedly pressing necessity for the construction of at least two or three first-class, dry docks at different ports in Canada.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: Where is it proposed to build these docks?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: One is needed at St. John, one at Halifax, one at Vancouver and one at Esquimalt.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: When I was Minister of Public Works there were in the department plans for one at Sydney.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: That is not a first-class dock.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
I might mention this fact as showing the difficulty of securing capital for the building of a dry dock based simply upon a subsidy that expires at a certain time, where the principal is not
44"i6

guaranteed. For a good many years the law provided that if there was any cessation of operation of a dry dock, the subsidy should cease. I remember a gentleman from Halifax came to see me, and Mr. George Robertson, President of the Company dry dock at St. John came to see me a good many times, and he was also over to England many times, in connection with the project. They stated that the bonds might go into the hands of estates, widows and children, and they asked: What do they know about operating a dry dock? They said that unless the matter was made absolutely unconditional, those parties would not invest. The Hon. Mr. Fielding, when Minister of Finance, saw the possibility of that, and he introduced a Bill changing the law so as to make it absolutely unconditional, that whether the dry dock was operated or not, the subsidy should run' on for 35 years.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: That was after it was finished.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
Yes, but the Government might take charge of the dry dock and operate it, and charge up the company with the expenses and credit them with the receipts. Even with that change there has been very little result. What I have heard from people who have been speaking about investing is that in financing an enterprise which would run to about $500,000 and perhaps a larger amount, if a shipbuilding plant were established they would certainly want to issue their bonds during construction. What they have said to me-and I can see the reasonableness of it-is that providing a subsidy does not really aid very much the raising of money because they 'say that after the contractor or the company has put a million dollars into the work, if construction should cease and the subsidy should cease, the bonds would be of no value and the investor would be deprived of any security. They say that no bonds could be floated under those circumstances. My honourable friend will see how weak a security that would be. No. investor would take the bonds unless he was absolutely assured, beyond all possible question, that the dock would be completed. It would be in the public interest that some of these first-class dry docks should be constructed, and it would not be unreasonable to agree unconditionally to pay the subsidy up to 75 per cent, of the work during construction, particularly when a million dollars had actually been expended.

Then the Government would have the security of the $250,000. and also of whatever amount was taken as security from the contractor that the dock would be completed. With the site of the dock, the plant, and what was invested, there would not be very much likelihood of the public suffering to any extent. Of course, all my observations are based upon the idea that it is in the public interest that the docks should be constructed in places where the minister might decide it is desirable they should be constructed. With regard to railway subsidies there is a cash bonus of $6,400 per mile, but if the railroads were to stop in the forest after ten, twenty, or thirty miles were built, whatever money was put in would, to a certain extent be jeopardized1. Still it is good policy. If you are going to assist a public work, like a dry-dock, by a subsidy during construction, you must give something substantial. You are not giving them the principal, according to my idea; you are only giving them the interest for thirty-five years, and if by any misfortune the contractor should not be able to go on, the investor who has taken the bonds up to seventy-five per cent of what has actually been invested would have no security whatever. He would lose his interest for all the remaining thirty-five years. I would think that, particularly in those days, no investor would look at bonds for a moment unless the company actually had the money. I think in changing the law now and under these ciroum stances Parliament should be a little generous, and run some little risk, particularly where there would be a large margin which would be provided if the security was only given up to seventy-five per cent of construction. My fear is that nothing will be accomplished if the Bill goes through as the minister now proposes, and ,1 speak from my experience as a minister, and my knowledge as a solicitor of a company some years ago, knowing how wary investors are in regard to a security of this nature. In the first place, they say, that the principal is not secured, that all they get is interest, and not a high rate of interest. Everybody will admit that four and a half per cent is a low rate of interest to-day. Then they say: "If for any reason the dock should not be operated, our security is gone." We know Mr. George Robertson went to England and to the United States, and got promises everywhere, but when they came to look into the quesr tion, they said " It was defective, that it did not afford a security that was attractive and they would have nothing to do with it."
\

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: You mean if they get the principal and the interest guaranteed, it would be possible to find people to take up the investment?

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: No, they never had the principal guaranteed and they will not, under my proposal. All they would have would be the interest guaranteed for thirty-five years.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: On three-quarters of the principal.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: On three-quarters of the principal, that is all. I remember years ago the minister used to say to George Robertson, then mayor of St. John: any man will lend money at three peT cent; always forgetting the principal was never guaranteed, and was always in jeopardy.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: This resolution provides for thirty-five years' interest.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: It does, and the minister evidently has the view that it will be likely to make it easier for the investor or for the company if when $500,000 has been expended the minister may give a subsidy upon seventy-five per cent of that amount during construction. The difficulty is that under the resolution as it is, if the company issues its bonds for seventy-five per vcent of the $500,000, and if for any reason it is not able to go ahead, the man who has taken the bonds loses his security absolutely. He might get his interest for two years, or three years possibly, but if at any time the company should fail to go ahead, the security becomes waste paper, and therefore the investor would not have anything to do with it. I am satisfied it will be found that is the obstacle which will confront any company. I would like very much to see legislation which would bring results. There is no hse putting legislation on the statute books and thinking you are going to accomplish something, if, as a matter of fact, nothing will be accomplished. I have pointed out to the minister the difficulty which appears to me, and I hope that the minister and the committee may see their way clear to make some change .and give more security to the investor for bonds issued under construction.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
I would not undertake to say that the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John is not quite substantial, but at the same time it does not strike me as being a forcible one. There should not be any such thing as failure in
'the construction of a dry dock where there is a guarantee of four and a half per cent interest for thirty-five years. Such a thing should not be possible. I say this for the reason that before the Government enters into an agreement it should be absolutely certain that the agreement is with a company or a person who cannot fail to carry it out. There should be deposited with the Minister of Public Works one-quarter of the estimated cost of the undertaking. If it is to cost $3,000,000, there should be a deposit of $750,000, and the contractor should be able to put up that amount before he gets the contract. The member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) says it is difficult to get men to put money into dry docks. That is perfectly true, but it is not because the Government does not offer sufficient assistance. The difficulty is that it is a risky undertaking. None of the dry docks in the United States ever made a cent until recent years. The great trouble is tha* many dry docks have been built which shou'd not have been built, and in places where they should not have been built. I do not believe that you could find a dry dock on the Atlantic seaboard which had earned any interest whatever until five years ago. Great care should be exercised in entering into any contract for the cor.*tr,ict'Ci: of a dry dock anywhere. It does not follow that because the citizens of a place want a dry dock, they should get it, or because the Government is approached by contractors who want to construct a dry dock, they should receive a contract. That is one of the troubles with our Dry Dock Act,.
The statute makes an offer to the public to pay four and a half per cent interest on three-quarters orf the cost of the work for a limited period. This is an inducement to promoters to organize companies to construct dry docks whether they can or cannot possibly pay. I quite agree that there should be some dry docks in Canada. I do not know how the Pacific coast is provided at the present moment. I would not think it would be desirable to put a dry dock at Esquimalt and one at Vancouver. It would seem like a great waste of public money as probably the enterprises would hardly pay interest on the construction cost. It would not be fair to Vancouver, say, to erect another dry dock at Esquimalt because there is not enough business for two unless one was supported by the British Admiralty for naval purposes. I think the British Admiralty might very well be asked to do something with Tespect to a dry dock on the Pacific coast and also one on the Atlantic coast. I think it is quite apparent that

there should be a dry dock somewhere on the Atlantic cost with a capacity sufficient to meet the maximum demand on the Atlantic seaboard. Whether a dry dock will pay on the Atlantic coast is a debatable question. Whether a dry dock is an aid or encouragement to a shipbuilding plant is also another debatable question. Many ship builders say that they would not have a 83,000,000 dry dock if it were given to them for nothing. They say it is a separate industry altogether and that one does not help the other but that one is rather a disadvantage to the other. Therefore, I say in the interest of Canada that great care should be exercised by the minister in granting aid under this Bill when it becomes law. A first class dock is necessary, I would say, in the port of Halifax. It would be quite natural that I should suggest that. I would make that statement anyway whether I was representing the constituency of Halifax or not. Before the minister enters into a contract with anybody he should make sure that it is a reputable firm and he should not have in his mind the possibility of the company failing. I would not enter into a contract with any person who could possibly fail. He should give security to the Government for a quarter of the cost and the minister should provide that he is amply secured beyond all peradven-ture. Therefore, I do not take ve^y kindly to the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), namely, that we should undertake to pay interest upon a portion of 'the investment made in partial construction of a dry dock when the company has failed to complete its contract. The ' Government or somebody else, must come in and produce the requisite capital to complete the undertaking. I think that could he provided against by making sure that no contract should ever be made with any company that could possibly fail and which was no.t in a position to carry out its contract.
I quite agree with the purpose of the resolution in increasing the rate of interest. It is quite true that private capital will hardly embark in a drydock to-day of any size without some assistance. The rate of interest has risen during ithe war to such a height, and it is likely it will continue so for many years afterwards, that the Government is amply justified in increasing the rate from four to four and a half per cent.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
My idea is exactly like that of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that the Government should, and no doubt would, take ample security to en-
sure the completion of the drydock. There would be a margin of 25 per cent and there would be security put up in addition. The idea of giving a subsidy during construction is that the company could issue bonds against that which would be placed with its bankers. The bankers in turn want to put their bonds out amongst their clientele. They do not want to know the relationship between the company and the Government, or what security the Government has taken, but what they want to know is that beyond peradventure they can get their interest for a certain definite period. That is necessary, and that has been found necessary, in order to float these securities. It was a fact that for a number of years the subsidy might cease if the company ceased to operate the drydock. That prevented capital being raised. In view of the fact that a drydock can not be constructed in any place where it is not found by the minister, from the report of the officers of his department, to be in the public interest that it should be built, in view of the fact that the minister could always get this margin of 25 per cent and could have security which would be ample to ensure the construction of the dock, I would not think it would be unreasonable to allow the payment of interest upon 75 per cent of the expenditure during construction, provided, of course, that in each case the expenditure must reach at least $1,000,000. That in itself would be evidence of the financial ability of the company. Before it would get any subsidy at all it must expend $1,000,000 and so on practically through the construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: Is that the only amendment the hon. gentleman would make?

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: There is an amendment which occurs to me to be necessary because I have understood that there is a question even now under the present law as to whether in the case of a dock that is completed, passed by the engineers and accepted by the Government, and should cease, to receive its subsidy-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: That is after it is completed?	i

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
Yes. A change was made when Mr. Fielding was Minister of Finance with the intention of making the payment of the subsidy absolute. The moment the dock was completed, passed by the engineers, approved by the minister and adopted by the Governor in Council, no matter what happened after that the

subsidy would be continuous and indefeasible for the period of the subsidy under the contract. I have been told that some question has been raised. Indeed, I was informed that a sub-committee of council had expressed the opinion that notwithstanding the legislation intended to bring about that result, it was not clear from the statute that it was brought about. I would like if the minister would look into that and see that the spirit and intention of the legislation introduced by Mr. Fielding is absolutely carried out; so that, when a dock is once accepted as being built in accordance with the specifications, there should be no question of the payment. It is absolutely essential that any doubt should be removed.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: If the minister finds it necessary to redraft the clause, I should like to see something inserted to provide a guarantee that the work will be completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: That is provided in the Bill founded upon the resolution. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) does not appreciate the difficulties we have had in securing much, if any, result from the Dry Docks Subsidies Act apart from the floating dock at Montreal and the small dock ait Port Arthur, and his suggestion that parties intending to construct dry docks should be obliged to put up as a guarantee of good faith $750,000 would undoubtedly place such a barrier in the way that it would be impossible for us to get any results, even under the amended Act.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: All I meant was that such companies should be in a position to make it clear to the Government that they can supply the capital required above the proceeds of the bonds guaranteed by the Government to meet the total cost of the undertaking.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: That is in the existing Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
It goes without saying that the Government will guard against that. My hon. friend suggests that we should be careful not to have constructed in various parts of Canada dry docks under this Act unless they are absolutely necessary. I can assure my hon. friend that there is not much danger of the Act being abused in that way. There is little chance of having dry docks constructed unless there are very strong hopes of their being paying investments and being necessary, not alone in the public interest, but in the interest of the corporations or companies
undertaking their construction. The Dry Docks Act has been in force for some years, but its terms have not been sufficiently inviting to induce investors to undertake the construction of dry docks. My hon. friend suggested that he did not believe that there was necessity for a dry dock at Vancouver and also one at Esquimalt. My hon. friend does not realize the importance of our great western outlet through Vancouver and Esquimalt. Vancouver is probably the third largest port in Canada, and it has been greatly handicapped owing to the absence of a dry dock.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: I did not suggest that there should not be a dry dock at Vancouver. I understood it was suggested that there should be two first-class dry-docks on the western coast, one at Vancouver and one at Esquimalt. All I did was to suggest doubt as to the advisability of constructing two first-class dry-docks on. the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
In my humble judgment there is necessity for two, one at Vancouver and one at Esquimalt. Esquimalt is a very important port in that the Admiralty land all their ships there, and have been pressing for years for the construction of a dry dock. The Government have already taken up the question of securing the necessary land and preparing to carry out such construction if application should be made under the Dry Dock Subsidy Act. When I was in England I had occasion to take this matter up with Sir Edward Carson, who was then the head of the Admiralty, and the matter was gone into very fully by that department. I was at that time urging upon the Admiralty that it was their duty to build dry docks, not only at Esquimalt but also at Halifax, and I am glad to tell the committee that my proposals met with some favour, in fact, with a very great deal of favour, at the hands of Sir Edward Carson, who gave the matter very serious and thoughtful consideration.
We had some correspondence in the matter and the difficulty with Sir Edward Carson apparently was to be able to secure the necessary money from the Treasury Department, otherwise he would have been satisfied, upon the recommendation of the department, to carry out the construction of the docks at Halifax and Esquimalt. Hon. gentlemen can see the special interest the Admiralty appears to have in the necessity for docks at these two points.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
Was it intended that
the Admiralty should pay any part of the

44C2
expense at Esquimalt or Halifax, or was Canada to pay it all?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: My request of the Admiralty was that they should bear all the expense.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: Did they agree?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
I cannot say that they
directly agreed, but I pressed that point strongly.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: I understand the Government have taken over the docks at Halifax and Esquimalt and we now own them? Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: No, no,

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
At Halifax a company
owns the docks and the dock at Esquimau is owned by the Government.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: The Canadian Government owns whatever dock we have at Esquimalt?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
And we have owned
it for some time. Does the Government mean to go back to the old system of making it an Imperial dock, owned by the Imperial Government, instead of making it a Canadian dock?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
The dock at Esquimalt
is not sufficient to meet the requirements of the large ships which pass in and out at that point, and we have had the fact presented to us, times without number, that British vessels go to Seattle to have repairs made in dry dock at that American port. This has been the subject of discussion between us and the Admiralty for some time. When I was in London, I pressed upon the Admiralty that it was their duty to see that dry docks should be built at Esquimalt, and Halifax, and I am glad to say that 1 made an impression upon the department, represented by Sir Edward Carson, to the extent that he was willing to undertake the work, provided he could secure the money from the treasury, and it was referred to Mr. Bonar Law. I had two or three interviews with Mr. Bonar Law, and I pressed on him very strongly the necessity for providing funds for the carrying out of the construction of these two docks. I have not yet received a definite answer from him as to whether it will be possible to carry out the proposal which the Admiralty made, and to provide the necessary money.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
If they carry it out,
would the docks be open to the public, or would the use of them be confined to the Admiralty?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
The Admiralty would
naturally have first call, and no doubt they would be very glad to admit ships that would pay for the repairs and help reduce the expense. My argument with the Admiralty was that we had already started, and had under construction, a dry dock at Quebec; and also had one started at St. John; that we had given a subsidy for and secured a floating dock at Montreal, and another at Port Arthur; or, in other words, that we were providing the necessary dry docks for the ships that were doing the carrying trade of our country, and that it was the duty of the Admiralty to provide dry docks at points like Halifax and Esquimalt. That was the ground on which I based my argument, in endeavouring to secure approval of the proposition that the work should be undertaken by the British Admiralty, instead of the Canadian Government.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext: I think both the Admiralty and the Dominion Government gave aid to the company which owns the dry dock at Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
Yes, but it was a very small amount. My object in bringing this resolution before the committee was simply with a view to providing such subsidy as would secure the construction of first class dry docks wherever they are necessary. In respect to Halifax, we had a proposal from a very strong English company, a short time ago, and, in order to give the committee an idea of what The building of drydocks means, I may mention their estimate of the work incident upon the building of the dock itself, and the necessary shipbuilding plant that should go along with it, in order to make the dock a paying and profitable concern. The committee will appreciate that for years to come the great business, in my opinion, of this country will be that of building ships to carry the trade of our country. I had presented to me the estimates of this English company, to build a drydock and shipbuilding plant at Halifax, and their estimate amounted to something over $8,000,000. It runs into very, very large figures.
I am satisfied that whoever comes forward to take advantage of whatever subsidy this Parliament decides upon will undoubtedly represent strong interests, and I do not anticipate any difficulty, or any failure on the part of any company that would come forward in putting up the security necessary for the purpose of carrying such contracts to completion.

I am desirous to do whatever is best in the public interest, and I will not ask the committee to consider the resolution any further to-night, but to think it over tomorrow or next dlay, and see whether any useful amendment can be made. Our effort will be to secure some result from the legislation and the amendments which may be adopted. As no hon. gentleman desires to .say anything further, I move that the committee rise and report progress.

maintopic: DRY DOCK SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
As the Government, of which the hon. minister (Mr. Rogers) is so prominent a member, is now launching upon the doctrine and policy of public ownership, if we are going to own all the railroads in the country, what is the matter with owning the dry docks as well? I think the day will come-and it appears not 1 far distant-when the Government of Canada will own the railroads; and they will naturally own the ocean steamships as well. When they own ships in connection with their railways, they will certainly find dry docks very convenient, and if the doctrine of public ownership is to prevail in the [DOT]country, we might as well own the dry docks. After the war, I do not think the Government would have any difficulty in getting money at four or four and a half per [DOT]cent, perhaps cheaper, and if they could get it at three and a half or four per cent, it would be just as well for this House to own the dry docks, as to give four and a half per cent to somebody else, and not own the property.
The annual interest upon a dry dock costing $3,000,000 would be $135,000. For the thirty-five years, the interest would amount to $5,725,000. I suppose that we would need not less than five of them in Canada, two on the Pacific and three on the Atlantic. The interest upon these works for the thirty-five years would be $38,625,000. That is a very large amount of money to spend in connection with property that we do not own. I would suggest to the minister that if we are going to launch upon a policy of public ownership-ownership of railroads and all public utilities-we might as well own the dry docks with the rest.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C, J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 124 to amend the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act was read the second time and the House went into, committee thereon, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
On section 1-Making evidence of wife admissible in prosecution for non-support.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the effect of the amendment to the Canada Evidence Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The amendment is to add, in subsection 2 of section 4 of the Canada Evidence Act,, after the words "thirty-nine" in the fifth line thereof, the words "two hundred and forty-two A." Section 242A deals with the offence of non-support. By adding this section the effect of the provision is that the wife becomes a competent witness against her husband on a prosecution for non-support. The original section provides certain cases where the wife may be a competent witness against her husband. The present amendment simply adds to the existing cases of that kind the case of prosecution for non-support.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Cases of prosecution under the Criminal Code for non-support?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Yes.
On section 2-Penalty extended to foster parent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There is provision in the Criminal Code making seduction by masters or proprietors of factories-people in authority generally over the individual seduced- an offence without regard to the limitations of age that are made in ordinary cases. This is to include in this provision cases where there is seduction by the step-parent of the step child, the foster parent of the foster-child or the guardian of his ward. The position is thought to be analogous to the case of a person availing himself of a position of authority over a female child.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The section is very
desirable indeed.
On section 3- definition enlarged to include place where indecencies are practised :

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The effect of this
amendment is to add to the present definition of a bawdy house the words:
Or for the praotice of acts of indecency, or occupied or resorted to hy one or more persons for such purposes.
At present such a place is described as a house, room, set of rooms or place of any kind kept for the purpose of prostitution. It has been represented to us by different police authorities that there has unfortunately grown up in different cities under the guise of legi-
44C4

timate places of business -such as massage, etc.-establishments which are resorted to not for purpose of prostitution, but for the purpose of the commission of acts of indecency. It has been thought proper that they should be put on the same footing as the bawdy house.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
At the beginning of the session I brought to my honourable friend's attention a matter germane to that now under consideration. Some good ladies in Montreal have been trying to save young girls from the perils to which they are subjected. When such cases come before the Recorder's Court, the young girls are sent to an institution, under the direction of the nuns, and everybody knows that the young girls who come under the direction of the nuns are on their way to salvation. The trouble is that sometimes, when their term is up, they are met at the gate of the institution by the men or the women who have led them into their life of shame. If the minister could devise means further to protect those young girls by an amendment to the Criminal Code, that would certainly meet with the approval of the society.
Another point which has engrossed the attention of the good people in Montreal who take a special interest in the welfare of those poor creatures is that there should be an enactment whereby those cases could not be settled out of court, and also that the appeals should be restricted, especially in oases where the men or the women found in those institutions have previously been punished. In laTge cities like Montreal- and I suppose the case applies to all large cities-it is appalling to realize how many young women and especially young girls are taken away from their parents and become the victims of the white slave traffic.
I do not know if my hon. friend as Minister of Justice has taken into consideration the remarks I have made to him from time time, but it seems to me, if not at this session, at the next session, he should confer with those in authority at those large institutions and enact pretty drastic amendments to the Criminal Code. I have visited the Montreal institution on two occasions;
I know some good ladies who have given their- services to the protection of young girls, and they are very anxious that the work should not fail by any laxity in the criminal court, or in the regulations, or in the procedure which takes place either in the Recorder's Court, or before the Appeal Court. I simply wish to remind the minister that it would be the part of wis-
dom for him some day to review the legislation on this subject and to meet the views of the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I would remind my hOn. friend that it is not easy to find an adequate remedy for that state of affairs. The prisons and reformatories of this kind are not under the jurisdiction of this Parliament; they fall under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities. It was suggested to me at one time that some remedy could be brought about by providing for longer sentences for young women offending in the manner referred to, it being pointed out that the stay of a longer period would be more likely to bring about reform. At that time I did make some effort in the direction of endeavouring to feel my way towards the ' imposition of more severe punishment. I found that there was a very strong reaction against that because it was suggested that by increasing the term of imprisonment, whereas where you had a properly constituted institution where a real work of reform was carried on, the effects would be good, on the other hand, the power being limited to providing for longer sentence of imprisonment, we would not be able to discriminate between different institution's, and it might be unduly harsh to impose upon a young woman, who had made her first slip or started in	the
wrong path, a very long period of punishment. The objection was not conclusive to myself; but at the same time, at that time at all events, it did not seem possible to hope to put through legislation looking for a remedy by greater severity. No doubt if we could extend more widely the establishment of purely reformatory institutions, that would be of great advantage to the country.
With regard to those younger women falling into the hand? of those who had formerly led them into vicious courses, it is very difficult to deal with that from the point of view of criminal law. We have already upon the Statute Book very severe provisions with regard to anything in the way of white slavery or traffic of that kind, and we have in the .last few years strengthened the law. There is no doubt that the whole subject of how to deal with offenders of that class and how to surround them with the protection that ought to be afforded to them is one that should call for more consideration, for a real study and a remodelling of our provisions dealing with the matter. When opportunity occurs, if I should be in a position to deal with the

matter, I certainly would approach in a most sympathetic way the examination oi the question. At present I am afraid I cannot say more. I quite appreciate and sympathize with the suggestion the hon. member has made, and I believe the time will come when we shall be able to deal more satisfactorily with that most unfortunate class. In the meantime certainly every one must appreciate the work of the good ladies to whom the hon. gentleman has referred, who certainly deserve well of the country for the devotion they have shown for a long period to the good work of endeavouring t-o encourage those young women to improve. It is also fair to express a tribute of appreciation of the work of the good religious who are in charge of the institution to which the hon. member has referred. If the section is taken as carried, we might revert to the one about which the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) spoke.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-Penalty extended to foster parents:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The intention was to
add the step-parent or foster parent to the cases provided for. The law 'already provides for the case of the guardian who seduces his ward, and that is the reason why we repeal subsection (a) and replace it by the present subsection which includes, with the guardian who is already provided for, the step-parent or foster parent.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The old section is continued with this added. Is that what the minister means?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes, with the addition of foster parent or step-parent. The guardian is already in subsection (a).

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-Paragraph penalizing traders for not keeping books redrawn.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the present section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The present section contains -a provision just as it is here, save as regards the proviso that a man is not to l>
j convicted if the period for which he failed tc keep his books is more than five years anterior to the charge. The present section has been interpreted as providing that if at any time within the last five years he kept any books, he could not be convicted. What was in view under the old section, though it was unfortunately expressed, was that if
he had at any time during the last five years failed to keep such 'books of account he might be convicted. In view of the wording, it was interpreted to mean that only if, as as a matter of fact, for the whole period of five years he kept no books he might be convicted. The proviso here carries out the intention that he is not to be convicted if his offence of not keeping books is more than five years old.

speechtext: The increases are not .very large. This proposed tariff has been submitted to the different provincial authorities who are also interested in the question. maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Do I understand the
minister to say that there shall be a uniformity of constables' fees, that is, the provincial governments will enact or amend their scale of fees so as to have uniformity throughout the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Whether we are really the constitutional authority to fix the tariff ct not it has been the practice in the past under our law to fix the tariff for the services of constables in connection with criminal proceedings. It may perhaps be open to the question that being part of the administration of justice it would be more proper that the province should do it. As a matter of fact one of the provinces to which we submitted these changes did suggest that view. The tariff as established by the present Criminal Code has been accepted and acted upon, and the constables

have made representations to us, and the provincial authorities in some portions of the country at all events-Ontario notably-* have acquiesced in the representation that the fees paid those constables for services in connection with criminal matters were inadequate. The fees, of course, are not paid by the Dominion. In many cases they are paid by the parties. I think a glance at the fees will show they are not unduly large.
